# Judging Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* (Book I and the start of Book II) as an explanation

## 1. The question, frozen

The poem answers several things, but its title and opening make one central: **What is the physical world made of, and how do things come to be and pass away?** Range: everything we see — sea, land, sky, living things. It is asked as a forward question (what produces things?) with a blocked question inside it (why can nothing come from nothing?). Held there below.

## 2. The parts, in his own words

P1 Nothing is born from nothing. P2 Nothing returns to nothing. P3 Only two kinds of thing exist: bodies and void. P4 Primal germs (atoms) — solid, void-free, indivisible, eternal. P5 Unions of atoms (ordinary things). P6 The void (empty room). P7 Matter is endless in amount. P8 Space is endless; no centre, no bottom. P9 Atoms move by weight, by blows, and by a tiny **swerve** off the straight line. P10 Atoms differ in shape. P11 The senses are the ground of all belief.

**Jobs**, each as a contrast: kinds stay fixed, no sea-born men (J1); things come in fixed seasons (J2); things dissolve yet the whole persists (J3); things move at all (J4); equal-size things weigh differently (J5); nothing comes from nothing (J6); living things have some free play, not fixed fate (J7); the world does not fall into one heap (J8); each cow knows its own calf — shapes differ (J9). J1–J6 he **gives**; J7 and J8 he makes **requirements**; the free-will job is his own, and doubtful.

**Change list** (changes to the world the claim covers): take the void out; fill it; cut an atom in half; swap the seed that falls; move to any region of space; add or remove the swerve; supply more or less matter. Left out, silently: what atoms are made of, and how thought comes from them — those wait for later Books.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **Held** | Remove it: kinds and seasons lose their anchor (J1, J2). |
| P2 | **Held** | Remove it: the sum could not persist (J3). |
| P3 | **Held** | Remove "void": motion and weights fail (J4, J5). |
| P4 | **Held** | Soft germs cannot build iron or rock; he argues this himself. |
| P5 | **Held** | Compounded things dissolve; only unions break (J3). |
| P6 | **Held** | Same as P3 — nothing moves without room. |
| P7 | **Held** | Too little matter and the supply of blows fails (J8). |
| P8 | **Held** | Finite space and everything heaps at a centre (J8). |
| P9 swerve | **Held if** | Holds only the free-will job, which is his own and in doubt. Worse, he fixes no size and no place ("the least", "no fixed line"), so no change to the world could catch it out — its magnitude is **loose**. |
| P10 | **Held** | Remove the differences and no two calves or grains differ (J9). |
| P11 senses | **Borrowed** | Rests on an account of perceiving not tested here. |

Where the parts came from: P1–P8 and P10 are **built** — argued with the world in view and against rivals. P9 is nearer **asserted** (he admits the swerve can't be seen) and then fitted to free will. P11 is **borrowed**.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had things come from nothing, his account would break — it is not happy either way. That is its strength. But flip free will: if man had no free choice, the swerve would simply go and nothing else would notice. That part is loose.
- **Direction.** He answers "what produces it?", not just "what can we tell?". Fixed seeds *cause* the kinds. Sound.
- **Answer hidden in the start?** Not for atoms or void — both are argued from motion and weight. But the swerve is derived from a datum he merely asserts, and the senses are declared true while being used to prove themselves.
- **Pairs that pull.** The swerve pulls against the whole atomist law of fixed cause and effect: stronger, and the law weakens; weaker, and free will vanishes. He draws the line at "the least," and nothing shows where it belongs.
- **Catch-alls.** The swerve behaves like one: made as small as you please, it can never be caught. By this skill it needs a **gauge** — some reading that would show it doing its job. None is given.
- **Rivals.** Heraclitus (all fire), Empedocles (four elements), Anaxagoras (all in all). He beats each with a concrete change: soft elements can't make hard things; if everything is in everything, crushed grain would bleed. These jobs hold his atoms firmly. But strict **Democritus without the swerve** differs from him only on free will, and no change separates them. At this level they are one explanation.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

Give the swerve a gauge, or drop it: find one thing that should happen with it and not without it, and let its size be tested. Second, either test the claim that the senses cannot mislead, or mark it plainly as a borrowed plank. These are the two loose bolts.

## 6. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not the same as true. These atoms are indivisible and eternal; real atoms are neither. The account is tight at the joints, not correct in its facts. Its virtue is that it sticks its neck out and can be caught.

## 7. One next step

Put both halves of a poke to the swerve: name one change to the world that should make it larger, and one that should leave it alone. If neither can be run, mark it a label and say the free-will job has no support yet.
